title: Machine Learning Depth Check
description: Medium-to-very-hard machine learning interview questions based on the local notes, excluding deep learning.

questions.prompt: Suppose each of \(B\) regression trees has prediction variance \(\sigma^2\), and every pair of tree predictions has correlation \(\rho\). Assuming equal variance and correlation, what is the variance of their average?

choices.text: \(\sigma^2 / B\), regardless of \(\rho\)
\(\sigma^2\left[\rho + \frac{1-\rho}{B}\right]\)
\(\frac{\sigma^2(1-\rho)}{B}\)
\(\frac{\sigma^2\rho}{B}\)

questions.explanation: The average contains \(B\) variance terms and \(B(B-1)\) covariance terms. Dividing their sum by \(B^2\) gives \(\sigma^2[\rho+(1-\rho)/B]\), showing why reducing correlation is central to random forests.

questions.prompt: In a standard random forest with \(\mathtt{max\_features}=\sqrt{p}\), when is the random subset of candidate features normally sampled?

choices.text: Once for the entire forest
Once per tree and reused at every node
Independently at each split node of each tree
Only at the root node of each tree

questions.explanation: A fresh feature subset is normally drawn at every node. CART then chooses the best split only among those candidates, decorrelating trees throughout their structure.

questions.prompt: A target encoder is fitted once on the full training set before a random forest is trained. The forest's out-of-bag score is then reported. What is the central problem?

choices.text: OOB scoring cannot be used for classification
Each OOB row influenced its encoded features through its target, so the estimate leaks outcome information
Bootstrap samples contain only about 36.8% of the observations
Target encoding forces all trees to have identical bootstraps

questions.explanation: An observation is out-of-bag only with respect to a tree fit. If preprocessing used its target beforehand, the prediction is no longer out-of-sample. Encoding must be learned without the evaluated row, typically inside the resampling procedure.

questions.prompt: In weakest-link cost-complexity pruning, an internal node \(t\) replaces its subtree \(T_t\) at which effective \(\alpha\)? Let \(R\) denote training leaf risk and \(|L(T_t)|\) the number of subtree leaves.
questions.explanation: Pruning increases empirical risk by \(R(t)-R(T_t)\) while removing \(|L(T_t)|-1\) leaves. Their ratio is the \(\alpha\) at which the pruned and unpruned objectives tie.

questions.prompt: For binary gradient boosting that minimizes logistic cross-entropy using a logit-valued model \(F(x)\), what pseudo-residual is fitted at the current iteration?

choices.text: \(y-\sigma(F(x))\)
\(\operatorname{sign}(y-F(x))\)
\(\sigma(F(x))[1-\sigma(F(x))]\)

questions.explanation: The negative derivative of binary cross-entropy with respect to the logit is \(y-p\), where \(p=\sigma(F(x))\). A second-order method may also use \(p(1-p)\) as curvature.

questions.prompt: A second-order boosted tree approximates the loss in one leaf as \(Gw+\tfrac12(H+\lambda)w^2\), where \(G\) and \(H\) sum gradients and Hessians. Ignoring L1 regularization, what is the optimal leaf weight?

choices.text: \(\frac{G}{H+\lambda}\)
\(-\frac{H}{G+\lambda}\)
\(-\frac{G}{H+\lambda}\)
\(-\frac{GH}{\lambda}\)

questions.explanation: Differentiating the quadratic gives \(G+(H+\lambda)w=0\), hence \(w^*=-G/(H+\lambda)\).

questions.prompt: In binary AdaBoost, a weak learner has weighted error \(\epsilon=0.60\). What does its coefficient \(\alpha=\tfrac12\log[(1-\epsilon)/\epsilon]\) imply?

choices.text: It receives a negative coefficient, so its predictions are effectively reversed
It receives the largest positive coefficient so far
It receives coefficient zero
The coefficient is undefined because epsilon must be below 0.25

questions.explanation: An error above \(0.5\) makes \(\log[(1-\epsilon)/\epsilon]\) negative. Reversing a binary learner's predictions would instead give error \(0.40\).

questions.prompt: A strictly increasing transformation is applied to every score produced by a binary classifier. Which statement is necessarily true on a fixed dataset with no ties introduced?

choices.text: ROC AUC is unchanged, but probability calibration may change
Log loss and Brier score are unchanged
Accuracy at threshold \(0.5\) is unchanged
Expected calibration error is unchanged

questions.explanation: ROC AUC depends only on ranking, which a strictly increasing transformation preserves. Calibration and threshold-based decisions depend on the score values themselves.

questions.prompt: For a non-informative classifier whose ranking is random, what is the expected precision-recall AUC baseline approximately equal to?

choices.text: 0.5 for every dataset
The positive-class prevalence
One minus the positive-class prevalence
The squared positive-class prevalence

questions.explanation: Under random ranking, the expected fraction of positives among retrieved examples is the dataset prevalence. Unlike ROC AUC, the PR baseline changes with class balance.

questions.prompt: A classifier outputs perfectly calibrated probabilities. You want to maximize F1 on a deployment population. Why is threshold \(0.5\) not generally optimal?

choices.text: Calibration guarantees only ranking, not probability accuracy
F1 is a non-decomposable objective whose optimum depends on the score distribution and prevalence
F1 can only be optimized by an uncalibrated classifier
Threshold 0.5 always maximizes recall and therefore cannot maximize F1

questions.explanation: A \(0.5\) Bayes threshold is tied to equal misclassification costs for decomposable 0-1 loss. F1 couples decisions through aggregate precision and recall, so its optimal threshold is population-dependent.

questions.prompt: You use cross-validation to select hyperparameters and report the best candidate's mean score from those same folds. What is the most defensible correction when an unbiased performance estimate matters?

choices.text: Use nested cross-validation, with tuning confined to each outer training fold
Increase the number of hyperparameter candidates
Fit preprocessing on all data before cross-validation
Report only the best individual fold

questions.explanation: Selection exploits noise in the inner validation scores. An untouched outer fold estimates the performance of the entire model-selection procedure.

questions.prompt: A medical dataset has repeated visits per patient, and the model will be deployed on entirely new patients. Which split strategy best targets deployment performance?

choices.text: Randomly stratify visits so every fold has the same label rate
Place all visits from a patient in the same fold, while preserving temporal constraints if deployment is prospective
Duplicate rare-patient visits before splitting
Use leave-one-visit-out cross-validation

questions.explanation: Visit-level splitting leaks patient-specific information across folds. Grouping by patient matches the new-patient target, and a time-aware boundary is additionally needed for prospective deployment.

questions.prompt: Why is feature scaling usually important before ridge regression?

choices.text: Ridge is invariant to arbitrary rescaling of individual features
The \(L_2\) penalty acts on coefficient magnitudes, so feature units otherwise determine effective regularization
Scaling makes the \(L_2\) penalty equivalent to \(L_1\)
Unscaled data makes the normal equations mathematically undefined

questions.explanation: Rescaling a feature inversely rescales the coefficient needed for the same predictions, but the penalty changes. Standardization makes penalty strength more comparable across features.

questions.prompt: Two standardized columns of a design matrix are exactly identical. Under lasso regression, which statement is correct?

choices.text: Their two coefficients are always uniquely determined and equal
Predictions can be unique while coefficient allocation between duplicate columns is non-unique
Lasso must assign both coefficients to zero
The \(L_1\) penalty becomes strictly convex and ensures uniqueness

questions.explanation: Only the sum of the duplicate coefficients affects fitted values. Multiple allocations can have the same \(L_1\) norm and objective, so coefficients need not be unique even when fitted predictions are.

questions.prompt: Compared with pure lasso, why can elastic net be preferable when many predictors are strongly correlated?

choices.text: Its \(L_2\) component can encourage correlated predictors to enter or shrink together
It removes all regularization bias
It guarantees the globally correct causal variables
It is invariant to target leakage

questions.explanation: Lasso often selects one arbitrary member of a correlated group. Adding an \(L_2\) term stabilizes the solution and can produce a grouping effect while retaining sparsity from \(L_1\).

questions.prompt: In unregularized logistic regression, the classes are perfectly linearly separable. What happens to the maximum-likelihood estimate under ordinary assumptions?

choices.text: It has a unique finite solution at the maximum-margin hyperplane
Coefficient norms can diverge while likelihood approaches its supremum, so no finite MLE exists
All coefficients converge to zero
The Hessian becomes positive definite everywhere and forces convergence

questions.explanation: Scaling a separating vector increases confidence without misclassifying training points, continually improving likelihood toward a non-attained limit. Regularization restores a finite optimum.

questions.prompt: For an RBF-kernel SVM, what is the usual qualitative effect of decreasing \(\gamma\) while increasing \(C\)?

choices.text: Narrower kernels and stronger regularization
Wider, smoother kernel influence but a larger penalty for training violations
A linear kernel regardless of the new values
No change because gamma and C always cancel exactly

questions.explanation: Lower \(\gamma\) makes each example's radial influence broader, usually smoothing the boundary. Higher \(C\) penalizes margin violations more strongly, pushing toward closer training fit.

questions.prompt: Why must a proposed kernel generally produce a positive semidefinite Gram matrix for every finite input set?

choices.text: It ensures the kernel corresponds to inner products in some feature space and preserves convexity of the SVM dual
It ensures every feature vector has unit norm
It makes all training points linearly independent
It guarantees zero generalization error

questions.explanation: Positive semidefiniteness is the finite-sample signature of a valid inner-product kernel. It also makes the relevant quadratic optimization well behaved and convex.

questions.prompt: A naive Bayes text classifier receives two nearly duplicate features that are both highly predictive. What failure is especially likely?

choices.text: It may count essentially the same evidence twice and output overconfident posteriors
Its class-conditional likelihood becomes discriminative rather than generative
Its decision boundary must become nonlinear
Duplicate features are automatically removed by Bayes' rule

questions.explanation: Conditional independence is violated by duplicate signals. Their likelihood contributions multiply as if independent, often preserving useful rankings but exaggerating confidence.

questions.prompt: Among all rank-\(k\) linear reconstructions of centered data under squared error, which subspace does PCA select?

choices.text: The span of the \(k\) covariance eigenvectors with the smallest eigenvalues
The span of the \(k\) covariance eigenvectors with the largest eigenvalues
Any \(k\) original coordinate axes
The \(k\) features most correlated with an external target

questions.explanation: The leading eigenvectors maximize captured variance and, equivalently, minimize squared orthogonal reconstruction error among rank-\(k\) linear projections.

questions.prompt: One feature is measured in dollars with variance \(10^8\), and another in ratios with variance \(0.01\). PCA is applied to the covariance matrix without scaling. What is the main consequence?

choices.text: PCA automatically normalizes both features because eigenvectors have unit norm
The dollar feature can dominate leading components because PCA is sensitive to measurement scale
Both features contribute equally by definition
Only the feature with smaller variance can appear in the first component

questions.explanation: Unit-norm loading vectors do not standardize input variance. PCA on a covariance matrix emphasizes large-scale variables unless that scale is substantively intended.

questions.prompt: Why can unconstrained maximum likelihood for a Gaussian mixture be ill-posed?

choices.text: A component can collapse its covariance around one observation and drive likelihood toward infinity
Gaussian densities can never overlap
Mixture weights are required to be equal
EM always finds the global minimum instead of a maximum

questions.explanation: A component centered on a data point with vanishing covariance can assign that point unbounded density. Covariance floors, priors, or other regularization prevent this degeneracy.

questions.prompt: What phenomenon most directly undermines Euclidean k-nearest neighbors as irrelevant dimensions are added?

choices.text: Distances tend to concentrate, reducing contrast between near and far points
The triangle inequality stops holding
Euclidean distance becomes negative
The number of training examples automatically decreases

questions.explanation: In high dimensions, relative distance contrast can shrink, so the nearest point is not much nearer than typical points. Irrelevant coordinates amplify this curse of dimensionality.

questions.prompt: Under exact E- and M-steps, what does the standard EM algorithm guarantee at each iteration?

choices.text: The observed-data likelihood does not decrease, but convergence may be to a local optimum or saddle point
The global maximum is reached in one iteration
Every parameter changes by the same amount
The complete-data likelihood is maximized over latent variables and parameters jointly

questions.explanation: EM alternates a tight lower-bound construction and maximization, yielding monotonic non-decrease of observed likelihood. That guarantee is local, not global.

questions.prompt: Why is the Brier score called a strictly proper scoring rule for binary probabilistic predictions?

choices.text: In expectation, reporting the true conditional probability uniquely minimizes the score
It depends only on the ranking of scores
It is always numerically equal to classification error
It ignores calibration and measures only sharpness

questions.explanation: For squared probability error, the expected score is uniquely minimized by the true event probability. This rewards honest probabilistic forecasts, not merely correct rankings.

questions.prompt: Two features are strongly correlated and carry nearly interchangeable signal. Why can ordinary permutation importance misleadingly assign low importance to either one?

choices.text: After one feature is permuted, the correlated partner can retain much of the predictive information
Permutation importance retrains the model until both coefficients become zero
Correlated features cannot be permuted
Permutation importance measures only training runtime

questions.explanation: Marginally breaking one feature may have little effect when another feature substitutes for it. Grouped or conditional permutation schemes can address different notions of importance.

questions.prompt: What key modeling choice distinguishes interventional from conditional SHAP-style explanations for dependent features?

choices.text: Interventional methods break feature dependence when marginalizing missing features; conditional methods preserve dependence through a conditional distribution
Interventional methods never require model predictions
Conditional methods are defined only for linear regression
The two are always identical whenever features are correlated

questions.explanation: The background distribution encodes what 'missing' means. Breaking dependencies can evaluate unrealistic combinations; conditioning respects observed associations but changes the attribution semantics.

questions.prompt: Under ideal covariate shift, which relationship is assumed?

choices.text: \(P_{\text{train}}(x)\ne P_{\text{test}}(x)\), while \(P(y\mid x)\) remains the same
\(P_{\text{train}}(y)\) differs, but \(P(x\mid y)\) remains the same by definition
\(P(y\mid x)\) changes arbitrarily while \(P(x)\) is fixed
The train and test joint distributions are identical

questions.explanation: Covariate shift changes the input distribution while preserving the labeling mechanism. With support overlap, test risk can be estimated using weights \(P_{\text{test}}(x)/P_{\text{train}}(x)\).

questions.prompt: A classifier was trained under class prior \(\pi_{\text{train}}(y)\), but deployment has a different class prior while \(P(x\mid y)\) is unchanged. What shift is this, and what can be adjusted in principle?

choices.text: Label shift; posterior probabilities or decision rules can be corrected using estimated prior ratios
Pure covariate shift; no prediction adjustment is possible
Concept drift; only feature standardization is needed
No shift, because P(x|y) is unchanged

questions.explanation: Label shift changes \(P(y)\) while retaining class-conditional feature distributions. With identifiable priors and a suitable classifier, prior-ratio correction can update posteriors.

questions.prompt: In the causal graph \(X\to Z\leftarrow Y\), with no other path between \(X\) and \(Y\), what typically happens if you condition on \(Z\)?

choices.text: Conditioning opens the collider path and can induce a spurious association between X and Y
Conditioning blocks an otherwise open confounding path
X becomes a deterministic cause of Y
The graph becomes equivalent to X -> Y -> Z

questions.explanation: A collider blocks the path when unconditioned. Conditioning on the collider, or often one of its descendants, can create dependence between its causes.

questions.prompt: For \(Z\) to be a valid instrumental variable for estimating the causal effect of treatment \(X\) on outcome \(Y\), which combination is central?

choices.text: Z affects X, is independent of unmeasured X-Y confounders, and affects Y only through X
Z predicts Y perfectly and is caused by Y
Z is independent of X and directly affects Y
Z must be a post-treatment mediator between X and Y

questions.explanation: These are relevance, independence, and exclusion restrictions. Further assumptions, such as monotonicity, are often needed to identify a local average treatment effect.

questions.prompt: A team runs a conventional fixed-horizon p-value test every hour and stops the experiment the first time \(p<0.05\). Under the null, what is the main statistical issue?

choices.text: Repeated unplanned looks inflate the probability of at least one false positive above the nominal level
Optional stopping always makes the test overly conservative
The treatment effect necessarily becomes negative
The p-value becomes a Bayesian posterior probability

questions.explanation: A fixed-horizon threshold does not control type-I error under continuous peeking. Preplanned group-sequential boundaries, \(\alpha\)-spending, or always-valid sequential methods are appropriate alternatives.

questions.prompt: A regression dataset contains a few very large residuals. Compared with MAE, how will RMSE usually react?

choices.text: It will be less affected because square roots remove outliers
It will be more affected because residuals are squared before averaging
It will always equal MAE
It will ignore the largest residuals

questions.explanation: RMSE is \(\sqrt{\frac1m\sum_i e_i^2}\), so large residuals receive quadratic weight. MAE uses \(\frac1m\sum_i |e_i|\) and is generally more robust to outliers.

questions.prompt: The positive class represents 5% of a classification dataset. What is the main purpose of a stratified train/test split?

choices.text: Preserve approximately the same class proportions in each split
Guarantee identical feature distributions in each split
Place all positive examples in the test set
Remove the need for a validation set

questions.explanation: Stratification controls the label composition of each split, reducing the chance that a rare class is severely underrepresented by random sampling.

questions.prompt: Let \(X\) be symmetrically distributed around zero and let \(Y=X^2\). What can happen to Pearson correlation between \(X\) and \(Y\)?

choices.text: It must equal 1 because \(Y\) is determined by \(X\)
It must equal -1 because squaring reverses negative values
It can be near zero despite a deterministic nonlinear relationship
It is undefined for every symmetric distribution

questions.explanation: Pearson's \(r\) measures linear association. Symmetry can make positive and negative linear contributions cancel even though \(Y\) is completely determined by \(X\).

questions.prompt: Where should a median imputer learn its per-feature medians when evaluating a model?

choices.text: From the combined training and test data
From the training data only, then reused to transform validation and test data
Independently from each individual test row
Only from rows that contain no missing values anywhere

questions.explanation: Fitting the imputer on validation or test data leaks information about those distributions. The learned training medians should be reused for every later transform.

questions.prompt: Which expression describes standardization using training-set statistics?

choices.text: \(z=x-\sigma_{\text{train}}\)
\(z=(x-\mu_{\text{train}})/\sigma_{\text{train}}\)

questions.explanation: Standardization subtracts the training mean and divides by the training standard deviation. Unlike min-max scaling, it does not force values into a fixed range.

questions.prompt: A classifier produces \(TP=80\), \(FP=20\), and \(FN=40\). What is its precision?
questions.explanation: Precision asks what fraction of predicted positives are correct: \(\text{Precision}=TP/(TP+FP)=80/100=0.80\).

questions.prompt: As the decision threshold of a fixed binary score model increases, which behavior is generally correct?

choices.text: Recall must increase and precision must decrease
Both recall and precision must increase
Recall cannot increase; precision often increases but can occasionally decrease
Neither metric can change

questions.explanation: Raising the threshold can only remove predicted positives, so recall is non-increasing. Precision often improves, but removing a true positive can make it fall locally.

questions.prompt: How many binary classifiers does a one-versus-one strategy train for \(K=8\) classes?
questions.explanation: One-versus-one trains a classifier for every unordered class pair, giving \(K(K-1)/2\) models.

questions.prompt: Why can gradient descent converge slowly when input features have very different scales?

choices.text: The loss automatically becomes non-convex
The objective can become an elongated bowl, causing inefficient zig-zagging
The gradient becomes exactly zero at initialization
Feature scaling removes all local minima

questions.explanation: Unequal scales can make curvature badly conditioned. A single learning rate then progresses slowly along shallow directions while oscillating along steep ones.

questions.prompt: Why is a decreasing learning schedule often used with stochastic gradient descent?

choices.text: Large early steps explore quickly, while smaller later steps reduce oscillation near a minimum
It makes every stochastic gradient equal to the full-batch gradient
It guarantees convergence to the global optimum for every non-convex loss
It removes the need to shuffle training examples

questions.explanation: Single-example gradients are noisy. Decaying the step size retains fast early movement but allows later updates to settle more closely around a minimum.

questions.prompt: A learning curve shows training and validation errors that are both high and close together after using all available data. What is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.text: Severe target leakage
High variance that more regularization will worsen
High bias or underfitting
Perfect generalization

questions.explanation: When both errors plateau at similarly poor levels, the model cannot fit even the training data well. More data alone is unlikely to fix this high-bias pattern.

questions.prompt: What is the usual bias-variance effect of increasing regularization strength?

choices.text: Lower bias and higher variance
Higher bias and lower variance
Lower irreducible error
No effect unless the target is categorical

questions.explanation: Stronger regularization restricts model flexibility. This usually increases approximation bias while reducing sensitivity to the particular training sample.

questions.prompt: In a soft-margin SVM, what is the usual effect of decreasing \(C\)?

choices.text: Margin violations become more costly and the margin narrows
The kernel is removed
Every training point must become a support vector
Margin violations become less costly, usually allowing a wider, more regularized margin

questions.explanation: A smaller \(C\) places less weight on hinge-loss violations relative to margin size, so the classifier tolerates more violations in exchange for stronger regularization.
questions.reference: P1-ml-oreilly.md — Support Vector Machine and the separation problem

questions.prompt: A binary classification node contains class proportions \(0.8\) and \(0.2\). What is its Gini impurity?
questions.explanation: Gini impurity is \(G=1-\sum_k p_k^2\). Substituting the two proportions gives \(1-0.64-0.04=0.32\).

questions.prompt: What distinguishes bagging from pasting when constructing each learner's training subset?

choices.text: Bagging trains sequentially; pasting trains in parallel
Bagging samples only features; pasting samples only labels
Bagging samples observations with replacement; pasting samples without replacement
Bagging is for regression; pasting is for classification

questions.explanation: Bootstrap aggregation draws with replacement, so a row can appear multiple times. Pasting constructs subsets without replacement.

questions.prompt: When a bootstrap sample of size \(m\) is drawn from \(m\) observations, approximately what fraction of observations are out-of-bag for one learner?
questions.explanation: The probability a row is never drawn is \((1-1/m)^m\), which approaches \(e^{-1}\). The complementary \(63.2\%\) is the expected unique in-bag fraction.

questions.prompt: Why should a stacking meta-learner usually train on held-out or out-of-fold base-model predictions?

choices.text: To force all base models to make identical predictions
To make hard voting equivalent to soft voting
To eliminate the need for a final estimator
To prevent the meta-learner from exploiting overly optimistic in-sample base predictions

questions.explanation: Base models can look unrealistically accurate on their own training rows. Out-of-fold predictions give the meta-learner features that better resemble inference-time behavior.

questions.prompt: What does setting \(\operatorname{PCA}(\mathtt{n\_components}=0.95)\) request in scikit-learn?

choices.text: Keep the smallest number of components whose cumulative explained variance is at least 95%
Discard exactly 95% of the original features
Keep components with individual variance greater than 0.95
Use 95 principal components regardless of the data

questions.explanation: A fractional component setting is an explained-variance target. PCA chooses enough leading components to reach the requested cumulative proportion.
questions.reference: P1-ml-oreilly.md — PCA and How to choose the number of dimensions

questions.prompt: Why does k-means commonly run several initializations and keep the result with the lowest inertia?

choices.text: Each initialization uses a different value of \(k\)
Inertia is guaranteed to be identical across initializations
Different starting centroids can converge to different local solutions
Multiple initializations make k-means density based

questions.explanation: K-means decreases inertia during a run but is sensitive to its starting centroids. Repeating initialization reduces the chance of retaining a poor local solution.

questions.prompt: Which serving setup best matches a fraud model that must score each transaction before authorization?

choices.text: A weekly batch job optimized only for throughput
Online serving optimized for low prediction latency
Offline training with no prediction endpoint
A precomputed table that never uses transaction context

questions.explanation: The decision is needed synchronously for each new transaction, making online low-latency serving the natural fit. Batch serving is better when predictions can be accumulated or precomputed.
questions.reference: system-design-ml.md — Model deployment and prediction serving
